lesson.title: Reading a chemical formula

steps.headline: What a formula says about one molecule

lead.text: Look at H₂O. The letters are chemical symbols, H for hydrogen and O for oxygen. The small number written low after a symbol is a subscript, and it says how many atoms of that element are in one molecule. So H₂O has two hydrogen atoms and, because the O has no number after it, one oxygen atom. A symbol with no subscript always means one atom.

Carbon dioxide, CO₂, follows the same pattern. Each molecule has one carbon atom and two oxygen atoms. In the last lesson's drawing, that carbon atom was joined to each oxygen atom by a double bond. A Lewis drawing shows how the atoms are joined, and the formula keeps only the count.

afterFigure.text: The picture lists the atoms in one molecule of each substance. Read the formula from left to right and each symbol gives you an element and its subscript gives you the count.

lead.text: Methane, the main gas in natural gas, has the formula CH₄.

A formula describes one molecule. To talk about several molecules, write a whole number in front of the formula. That number is the coefficient, and it says how many molecules there are. So 3 H₂O means three water molecules, each with its own two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom.

The kitchen order works the same way. Five boxes hold five times as much bread as one box. In a formula the small number says what is inside each molecule and the large number says how many molecules there are. They do different jobs, so you use both. To count the atoms of one element in the whole group, multiply the atoms in one molecule by the number of molecules.

afterFigure.text: In the picture, each CO₂ molecule has one carbon atom and two oxygen atoms. Two molecules hold 2 carbon atoms and 4 oxygen atoms, and four molecules hold 4 and 8. Doubling the coefficient doubles every count, because each extra molecule brings all of its atoms with it.

lead.text: Three water molecules sit in the picture. Decide which number tells you how many molecules there are and which tells you the atoms in each one.

reveal.text: You took the oxygen in one molecule and counted it once for every molecule. That is what a coefficient asks for.

steps.headline: How many hydrogen atoms are in 4 H₂SO₄?

workedSteps.text: Read the subscript: each H₂SO₄ has 2 H atoms.
Read the coefficient: there are 4 units.
Multiply the atoms in one unit by the units.

steps.headline: Count the oxygen atoms in 2 Al₂O₃.

workedSteps.text: The subscript after O is 3, so each unit has 3 oxygen atoms.

steps.headline: Counting every atom in the order

lead.text: Sometimes you want the total number of atoms, whatever element they belong to. Do it in two stages. First add up the atoms in one unit by reading each subscript, and remember that a symbol with no subscript counts as one. Then multiply the total by the coefficient.

Take 3 CaCl₂. In one unit there is 1 calcium atom and 2 chlorine atoms, which makes 3 atoms. Three units have 3 × 3 = 9 atoms. CaCl₂ is an ionic compound, so its formula gives a ratio of ions in a crystal and not a single molecule. The counting works the same way, and unit is the word for either kind of group.

afterFigure.text: The picture splits the same count by element, with 3 calcium atoms and 6 chlorine atoms. They add to 9, the same total as before, so you can count either way and use the other to check.

lead.text: The two numbers behave differently when you change them. Change a coefficient and you change how much of a substance there is. Change a subscript and you change the substance itself. H₂O is water. H₂O₂ has one more oxygen atom in each molecule, and it is hydrogen peroxide, a different liquid with different properties.

So to have more water, write a bigger number in front: 2 H₂O, then 4 H₂O. Every molecule is still H₂O. A subscript belongs to the identity of the substance, and you only change it when you mean a different substance.
Later lessons write whole chemical equations, and they need this rule. When an equation needs more of a substance, a coefficient supplies it and every formula stays exactly as it is.
Sulfuric acid is H₂SO₄. Add up the atoms in one unit first, then multiply by the coefficient.
Ammonia is NH₃. A missing subscript means one atom.

lesson.orientation: Separate subscripts inside a formula from coefficients multiplying whole units.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A school kitchen packs lunches in boxes. Every box holds 2 slices of bread and 1 slice of cheese. When a class orders 5 boxes, nobody writes out ten slices of bread and five of cheese. The order just says 5 boxes, and everyone knows what a box contains.

Chemical formulas work in the same way. The last lesson drew molecules and counted the shared pairs inside them. A formula is a much shorter label for one molecule, such as H₂O for water, and it records which atoms the molecule contains and how many of each. Put a number in front of the label and you are ordering that many molecules.
This lesson reads both numbers. It counts what is in one box first, and then what is in a whole order.

intro.promise: By the end you'll count the atoms of each element in something like 3 H₂O.
intro.whyItMatters: Every chemical equation is written with these two kinds of number.

recap.keyIdea: A subscript counts the atoms of an element in one unit, and a coefficient counts the units. Multiply the two to count the atoms of that element.

blocks.text: Back in the kitchen, the box was the formula and the order was the coefficient. You counted 8 hydrogen atoms in 4 H₂SO₄, 6 oxygen atoms in 2 Al₂O₃ and 14 atoms in all in 2 H₂SO₄. Each time you took the atoms in one unit and multiplied by the number of units.

recap.nextHook: Once you can count the atoms in a formula, you can weigh them, because every atom has a mass. The next lesson adds up atomic masses to find the mass of one molecule.

questions.prompt: How many oxygen atoms are in 3 H₂O molecules?
hints: Multiply the O subscript, which is one, by the coefficient.
Each H₂O contains one O atom.
Each water contributes one oxygen; count the water molecules.
questions.onCorrect: 3. Each H₂O has one oxygen, and the coefficient says there are three of them.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the oxygen in one molecule. The coefficient multiplies it.
That counts the hydrogen as well. The question asks about oxygen.

questions.prompt: How many oxygen atoms are represented by 2 Al₂O₃ formula units?
hints: Multiply the entire formula by two.
The O subscript is three.
Multiply 2 formula units by 3 O atoms per unit.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each unit has three O atoms: 2 × 3 = 6.

questions.onCorrect: 6. Each unit has three O atoms, and there are two units.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the oxygen in one unit. There are more than one unit.
That adds the numbers. Atoms per unit and units multiply.

questions.prompt: To double an amount of water without changing the substance, what do you change?
hints: Keep the formula of each molecule fixed.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A coefficient multiplies whole water molecules.

questions.onCorrect: The coefficient counts molecules, so double it. Changing a subscript would change the substance.

misconceptions.feedback: Changing a subscript changes the molecule itself, so it is no longer water.
Changing the element symbol makes a different substance.

questions.prompt: How many hydrogen atoms are in 5 NH₃ molecules?
hints: Each ammonia molecule contributes three H atoms.
The H subscript is three.
Multiply 5 molecules by 3 H atoms per molecule.
questions.onCorrect: 15. Each NH₃ has three H atoms, and five molecules have five times as many.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the hydrogen in one molecule, not in all five.
That adds the numbers. Multiply the hydrogen in one molecule by the molecules.

questions.prompt: How many chlorine atoms are represented by 4 MgCl₂ formula units?
hints: Apply the coefficient to chlorine too.
The Cl subscript is two.
Multiply 4 formula units by 2 Cl atoms per unit.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each unit contributes two Cl atoms: 4 × 2 = 8.

questions.onCorrect: 8. Each MgCl₂ has two Cl atoms, and there are four units.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the chlorine in one unit. There are more than one unit.
That adds the numbers. Multiply them.

hints: Read the outside number separately from the inside number.

acceptedIdeas: Two molecules with two H atoms each
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The coefficient counts molecules and the subscript counts atoms per molecule.

choices.label: One molecule with four bonded H atoms
Two molecules with two H atoms each

questions.onCorrect: The coefficient counts molecules and the subscript counts atoms in each, so 2 H₂ is two molecules of two atoms.

misconceptions.feedback: The 2 in front counts molecules, so it does not join the atoms into one molecule.
The atoms in each molecule are bonded, not isolated.

questions.prompt: How many slices of bread are in the 5 boxes?
hints: How much bread is in one box?
Each box has the same amount.
Multiply the bread in one box by the number of boxes.
questions.onCorrect: 10. One box's contents times the number of boxes. A formula with a number in front works the same way.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the bread in one box. You bought more than one.
That adds the numbers. Multiply the bread in one box by the boxes.

questions.prompt: How many hydrogen atoms are in one molecule of CH₄?
hints: Find the small number after the H.
That is the subscript, and it counts that element's atoms.
There is one molecule, so nothing else multiplies it.
questions.onCorrect: 4. The subscript after H counts the hydrogen atoms in one molecule.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the carbon, which has no subscript. The question asks about hydrogen.
That counts every atom. The question asks about hydrogen only.

questions.prompt: Why do we multiply the subscript by the coefficient?

acceptedIdeas: The coefficient says how many units there are, and each unit has that many atoms
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Atoms in one unit times the units gives all the atoms.

choices.label: The coefficient says how many units there are, and each unit has that many atoms
The subscript tells us the number of molecules

questions.onCorrect: Right: each unit has the same atoms, so the total is atoms per unit times units.

misconceptions.feedback: The subscript counts atoms in one unit. The coefficient counts units.
This is only counting atoms. Balancing is a different job.

questions.prompt: How many atoms of all elements are in 2 H₂SO₄ (2 molecules of sulfuric acid)?
hints: Add up the atoms of every element in one H₂SO₄ first.
Read the three subscripts, and remember S has none.
Multiply that total by the number of units.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: One H₂SO₄ has 2 + 1 + 4 = 7 atoms, so 2 units have 14.

questions.onCorrect: 14. Seven atoms in one unit, and two units.

misconceptions.feedback: That is one unit's atoms. There are more than one unit.
That leaves out the sulfur. It has no subscript, so it counts as one atom in each unit.

questions.prompt: How many hydrogen atoms are in 3 C₂H₆ molecules?
hints: Find the subscript after H.
That is the hydrogen in one molecule.
Multiply it by the molecules.
questions.onCorrect: 18. Six hydrogen atoms per molecule, three molecules.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the hydrogen in one molecule. There are more than one.
That adds the numbers. Multiply the hydrogen in one molecule by the molecules.

The coefficient counts molecules and the subscript counts atoms per molecule.
The subscript after H is 4.
Atoms in one unit times the units gives all the atoms.

A subscript counts the atoms of an element in one molecule, and a symbol with no subscript stands for one atom.
The subscript after a symbol counts that element's atoms in one molecule.
A coefficient counts whole molecules, so the atoms of an element are the subscript times the coefficient.
Each H₂O has one oxygen atom, so three molecules have three.
Atoms of an element are its subscript times the coefficient: 4 × 2 = 8.
Each Al₂O₃ unit has three oxygen atoms, so two units have six.
The atoms in one unit are the sum of its subscripts, and the whole order has that many times the coefficient.
A coefficient sets how much of a substance there is, while a subscript is part of which substance it is.
All the atoms in the order are the atoms in one unit times the coefficient.
Each NH₃ has three hydrogen atoms, so five molecules have fifteen.
